report.headline: Usage rate projected to fall from 28.9% (+1.85 sd) in the EuroLeague to 23.3% in the NBA, just above the 20.0% league average; the shooting-efficiency projection carries no information.

projection.text: The model projects a usage rate of 23.3% in the NBA, down from 28.9% (+1.85 sd) in the 2017-18 EuroLeague season, placing the subject just above the target league's minutes-weighted average usage of 20.0%.

risks.text: The source-season sample is thin: only 33 games and 856 minutes, a limited base for the production rates cited.
Shot selection was extreme, with 50.0% of attempts taken from three, a profile that may not hold or may not translate efficiently against NBA rim protection and defense.

The true shooting projection of 55.3% is not reliable: the model's error (4.7%) matches the trivial baseline's error (4.7%), meaning it offers no edge over simply guessing the league average for this metric.

Even the informative usage-rate projection carries real uncertainty: the 80% interval (18.0%-28.5%) and 95% interval (15.3%-31.3%) are wide relative to the NBA's usage standard deviation of 5.2%, so an individual outcome could land well below or above the point estimate.

strengths.text: Source-season usage was extreme at 28.9%, +1.85 sd above the EuroLeague average, alongside a 29.8% assist rate and 5.97 assists per 75 possessions, indicating a heavily involved offensive role.

True shooting was 61.2% in the source season, +0.39 sd above the EuroLeague average, while also producing 6.727 rebounds per 75 possessions, suggesting efficient scoring alongside secondary rebounding.
Turnover rate was a modest 15.0% despite carrying a 29.8% assist rate and 28.9% usage, a favorable ratio of playmaking load to giveaways.
The subject was 18.0 years old in the source season, unusually young for the production recorded.

uncertainty.text: The 80% prediction interval for usage rate runs 18.0%-28.5% and the 95% interval 15.3%-31.3%, spanning most of a single NBA usage standard deviation (5.2%); the model still beats a naive league-average baseline on this metric (MAE 3.3% vs 4.3%), so it ranks players but cannot pin down this one precisely. The true shooting projection of 55.3% (80% interval 49.5%-61.2%, 95% interval 46.4%-64.2%) should not be trusted at all: its MAE (4.7%) is no better than the trivial league-average baseline (4.7%), so the model has nothing useful to say about shooting efficiency here. The estimate is drawn from 61 historical EL->NBA transitions, and those who made the move typically sat +0.46 sd above their own league already, so this is conditional on the move happening, not a league-average expectation.
